painpoints.name: Accurate 3D ground truth needs instrumentation that alters the scene
painpoints.statement: Accurate 3D ground truth for hands, bodies and manipulated objects can still be obtained only with markers, gloves, IMUs, robot arms, anti-reflection coatings, dense calibrated camera domes and manual correction, which alter appearance and motion, fail under contact and occlusion, cannot follow moving objects at scale and confine capture to labs, so realism and annotation accuracy cannot be obtained together.
painpoints.description: Hand-object and body-object dataset papers describe a trade-off between realism and accuracy: optical markers are lost, merged or mislabelled under occlusion and contaminate RGB, gloves change hand appearance, inertial suits drift, and markerless domes need 20 to 170 cameras, per-object scans and manual cleanup, with error growing two- to three-fold as views are removed (ARCTIC hand error 23.4 to 49.0 mm from 8 to 2 views). Object-pose papers describe the same trade-off for static labels, where robot arms and IR trackers are accurate but limit viewpoints and backgrounds and SfM or ARKit alignment scales but leaves centimetre errors. Moving objects are harder: markers cannot be used, mocap confines capture to rooms, and tracker propagation drifts and needs manual fixes every ten frames. As a result, datasets are table-scale, single-room or single-site, and in-the-wild datasets lack dense 3D ground truth. Proposed fixes such as marker inpainting, mobile backpack rigs, hybrid optical-inertial capture, learned annotators and semi-supervised learning each give up accuracy, scale or naturalness.

evidence_items.item: MoCap marker data contain errors requiring manual cleaning; markers are lost under extreme occlusion, ghost markers appear and close markers merge or are mislabelled (same paper as 67).
Capture methods force a trade-off between motion accuracy and visual realism; vision and RGB-D capture are less accurate and occlusion-prone, IMU capture drifts.
Existing category-level datasets are either large but inaccurate or accurate but small with limited viewpoints; robot-based annotation limits viewpoints and backgrounds.
Marker-based annotation cannot be used on moving objects; BundleTrack is used instead but drifts and needs manual fixes every ten frames.
Markers on objects widen the appearance gap to in-the-wild objects and a tracker could learn markers instead of the object; marker removal by inpainting cannot recover true appearance.
There is a trade-off between environmental realism and 3D annotation accuracy; automated filtering discards hard frames.

painpoints.attempted_fixes: Marker inpainting, manual and artist cleanup, neural relighting, mobile backpack rigs, hybrid optical-inertial capture, smartphone arrays, SAM2 with manual correction, learned annotators, multi-view dynamic matching, robot-arm or stop-and-go capture, anti-reflection spray, tracker propagation with manual fixes, smoothed pseudo-labels and semi-supervised learning. Each trades accuracy, scale or naturalness, and manual work remains.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Measuring the occluded, moving, in-contact state of hands and objects requires sensors that touch or surround the scene, and those sensors are exactly what makes the scene unnatural and immobile. Without an independent measurement channel that is invisible to the camera, natural single-camera manipulation cannot be labelled at millimetre accuracy.

painpoints.name: Objects without a template or category prior
painpoints.statement: Without a pre-scanned mesh, CAD model or narrow category prior, the field cannot reconstruct and track the 6D pose and shape of an everyday object being handled: model-free onboarding from casual or hand-manipulation video falls far below model-based accuracy, category-level networks collapse as vocabularies grow, and human-object datasets and human-to-robot pipelines therefore restrict themselves to a few scanned rigid objects or release no object pose at all.
painpoints.description: Almost every hand-object and human-object dataset, method and tracker assumes a known template, often with markers or IMUs attached, and challenges cover one person with one object; the BOP 2024 model-free hand-manipulation onboarding track drew no submissions, and model-free FoundationPose scores 0.25 AR versus 0.67 with a CAD model. Template-free pipelines (HOLD, HOSt3R, Gaussian-splatting challenge entries) depend on fragile SfM or keypoint registration, assume one hand, a rigid unchanging grasp and curated clear-view frames, leave hand-occluded surfaces missing and fall far behind on bimanual sequences. Reference-based methods fail at uncovered viewpoints or with few references, reconstruction-based onboarding fails at range, and category-level methods fall from 62.52 to 14.42 percent 5deg2cm as categories grow from 3 to 48 and reach 3.24 percent on unseen categories. Egocentric robot-learning datasets release masks only, and pipelines that need object motion scan, multi-view-capture or generate a mesh and track it with FoundationPose. Shape retrieval, generated meshes with manual repair, on-the-fly templates and foundation shape priors are partial or only proposed.

Object poses are not annotated; object-centric affordance and manipulation models are left to future work, and annotating object poses is listed as future work.

All are offline, need curated frames or posed references, assume rigid grasps, or still need a mesh.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Without a model, pose and shape must be estimated jointly from partial views in which the hand hides the object, and correspondence-based registration breaks on exactly the textureless, small and occluded views manipulation produces; templates make the problem tractable, so datasets keep requiring them.

painpoints.name: Accuracy only offline: no causal real-time estimate
painpoints.statement: The most accurate hand, hand-object, human-object and unseen-object pose results depend on offline whole-sequence smoothing, per-sequence optimisation or seconds-per-frame inference, and no causal method of comparable accuracy runs in real time for uses that need live feedback, such as a robot reacting to a person during a handover, AR/VR or point-of-care assessment.
painpoints.description: Challenge-winning hand pipelines rely on non-causal Savitzky-Golay, Gaussian or Neural Smooth filtering, annotation and template-free reconstruction run tens of thousands of iterations or about a GPU-day per sequence, and joint human-object fitting still needs an optimisation layer (CHORE about 312 s per frame). The best unseen-object 6D methods take 24.9-34.6 s per image and unseen-object estimators run below 4 FPS (FoundationPose 0.98 FPS), diffusion pose and pressure models run at a few frames per second, and avatar and clinical pipelines fit each subject, sequence or trial offline. Real-time uses are named as blocked: cobot assembly and handover failure detection use future frames, and robot-assisted bathing cannot be used on people because online pose and shape estimation with sub-frame latency during contact does not exist. Regression replacing optimisation, faster proposal generators, sparse matching, distillation and lightweight architectures trade accuracy for speed or remain proposals.

Analysis is offline and post-hoc, with GPU optimization of a MuJoCo biomechanical model per trial; real-time point-of-care processing is open.
The system cannot be used on humans; perception is the main bottleneck, and online pose and shape estimation with sub-frame latency during sustained contact does not exist.

painpoints.settings: Egocentric hand tracking challenges (UmeTrack, HOT3D, AssemblyHands); ARCTIC template-free reconstruction; studio object tracking; monocular and RGB-D human-object fitting (BEHAVE, InterCap, RHOBIN); dense-dome HOI capture; multi-person global video optimisation (WorldPose); wearable LiDAR-IMU capture; BOP unseen-object 6D localisation and DynOPETs moving-camera sequences; avatar training and rendering in studio domes; clinical monocular reachable-workspace assessment; cobot assembly (ATTACH), handover failure detection (HFD) and robot-assisted bathing.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Offline smoothing filters and whole-sequence optimisation; regression networks replacing optimisation (RHOBIN entrants still keep an optimisation layer); fewer hypotheses and faster proposal generators (SAM6D at 3.87 s loses accuracy); sparse matching instead of visual localisation (fails on textureless objects); one-step and consistency distillation for diffusion; causal MS-TCN variants; hash-grid and 4D decomposed avatar representations; proposed lightweight models, faster deformers and mobile point-of-care pipelines. No causal method matching offline accuracy is reported.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Occlusion and depth ambiguity are currently resolved by looking at the whole sequence and iterating render-and-compare or physical constraints, which a causal per-frame method cannot do, and benchmarks reward offline accuracy without any latency budget.

painpoints.name: Pose of the handled object during manipulation
painpoints.statement: The 6D pose, and often the mask, of an object while a person grasps and moves it cannot be tracked reliably from egocentric, monocular or sparse RGB-D input: trackers that work when only the camera moves collapse once the hand grasps the object, hand-held recall stays near one third even multi-view with ground-truth masks, and joint human-object reconstruction leaves object errors of centimetres to decimetres, two to five times the body error.
painpoints.description: Dataset papers find object perception, not hand or body perception, to be the weakest link: BundleTrack, FoundationPose and FoundPose succeed under camera motion but fail once the object is grasped, BOP-H3 accuracy drops relative to static BOP, active-object segmentation lags hand segmentation by about 60 AP points, and whole-body HOI benchmarks report object error two to five times body error (BEHAVE 21.20 cm versus 4.99 cm). The causes named are hand or body occlusion of the object, rapid object motion, objects leaving the view, sensor noise, symmetric objects, small visible area and the absence of object keypoint detectors. Human-to-robot pipelines therefore induce object pose from the hand under a rigid-grasp prior, register only on occlusion-free first and last frames, or discard occluded clips. Multi-view input (about +8 points), ground-truth masks, mask-difference resets with manual SAM2 correction, rigid attachment to body joints, IMU initialization and optimization after regression have been tried; none brings hand-held object tracking near the no-interaction level. Most object pose datasets contain no hands at all, so the condition is barely measured and joint hand-object pose is left to future work.

Accuracy drops on BOP-H3 (egocentric, hand-held, AR/VR headset data) relative to BOP-Classic-Core; onboarding from dynamic hand-manipulation video remains largely unaddressed.

Direct fitting of SMPL and the object template to noisy, incomplete Kinect point clouds gets stuck in local minima (object 26.09 cm v2v); symmetric objects get the right surface fit but the wrong orientation; the proposed tracker still has 21.20 cm object error versus 4.99 cm for the body.

Object visual tracking is infeasible during manipulation due to persistent hand occlusion, so object pose is induced from the hand under a rigid-grasp prior; CoTracker point tracking drifts when large rotations occlude tracked points; registration assumes the first and last frames are free of hand occlusion.
Category-level pose tracking drops from 86.5 on NOCS to 19.3 on HOI4D bottle; trackers work when only the camera moves but fail when the hand interacts (occlusion, rapid motion, sensor noise).
Active object segmentation stays weak: object mask AP about 24-28 on VISOR even fully supervised, far below hand AP of about 92.

painpoints.attempted_fixes: Multi-view input and ground-truth masks; model-based trackers with mask-difference resets and manual SAM2 correction; rigid attachment of the object to nearby joints or a rigid-grasp prior induced from the hand; registration on occlusion-free keyframes; IMU initialization of objects; predicted orientation and contacts as fitting constraints and optimization after regression; contact-guided placement with retrieved meshes; markers on objects and dense rigs; discarding or excluding occluded clips. Joint hand-object estimation and hand labels from mocap plus parametric hand models are listed only as future work.
painpoints.why_it_persists: The holding hand or body covers exactly the object surface the tracker needs, object pose benchmarks were built on static hand-free scenes, and ground truth for moving hand-held objects is itself hard to obtain, so methods are neither trained nor scored on the condition.

painpoints.name: Synthetic data cannot replace real interaction data
painpoints.statement: Synthetic hand, body and object-pose training data cannot yet replace real captured data: synthetic-only training trails real training by large margins and saturates as data grows, synthetic humans are rendered without handled objects or real contact, and object pose models trained on PBR renders lose most of their accuracy on real sensors and arrangements.
painpoints.description: Benchmarks for egocentric HOI detection, interacting-hand pose and RGB-D hand pose report synthetic-only training far below real (VISOR mask AP 9.88 versus 45.33; RenderIH 13.50 versus 6.76 mm PA-MPJPE), with gains plateauing at a few million samples. The large synthetic human sets animate bodies independently from AMASS, paste unrelated GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion, remove object-dependent actions and keep a real-domain gap, and simulation-derived dynamics and muscle labels share it. PBR-trained object pose falls from 0.827 to 0.266 AP on real bins and from 76.4 to 8.9 recall on recreated YCB-V scenes, and gains on standard benchmarks may reflect dataset-specific domain randomisation. The causes named are photorealism, inaccurate grasps, no model of the approaching hand, composited lighting, missing forearm and scene context, clean depth without sensor artifacts, and baked lighting in reconstructed assets. Domain adaptation, mixing, neural relighting, physics-simulated grasps, heuristic noise models and domain randomisation reduce but do not close the gap.

painpoints.name: Metrics hide absolute error, contact, physics and task tolerance
painpoints.statement: Standard hand, body and object metrics (Procrustes-aligned or root-relative joint error, COCO AP, ADD at centimetre tolerance, Chamfer, R-precision, per-frame F1) do not verify absolute placement, true contact, temporal stability, physical plausibility or downstream task success, and many interaction test sets carry pseudo ground truth or none for what they claim to measure, so rankings can hide the failures that matter for manipulation.
painpoints.description: A survey states that evaluation is dominated by geometric metrics that do not establish contact or function and that Procrustes alignment conceals absolute errors; MPJPE-PA also hides lower-arm rotation and jitter, COCO AP rewards anatomically impossible keypoints, R-precision cannot separate methods, and a widely used PA-MPJPE function had a bug. Interaction benchmarks fall back on accumulated contact, cross-pair consistency or 2D mask proxies because instantaneous contact, depth and in-the-wild 3D ground truth are unavailable, and HOI capture sets evaluate tracking only qualitatively. A grasping study finds pose and reconstruction errors evaluated in isolation, 2D projection and rotation metrics poor predictors of grasp success, and centimetre tolerances short of sub-millimetre industrial and millimetre AR needs, while real-robot grasp success in clutter stays at 33-68 percent. Population-specific, angular, jitter and drift metrics, contact-aware and safety metrics, simulated grasp benchmarks and user studies have been proposed, and none is standard.

evidence_items.item: Evaluation is dominated by geometric metrics; contact, function, physics and state transitions are rarely assessed together, and Procrustes alignment conceals absolute errors.
MPJPE-PA is forgiving: methods fail on lower-arm rotations that MPJPE does not reveal, all exceed 23 deg angular error, and good MPJPE-PA does not give visually pleasing results.

Pose estimators and reconstructions are evaluated in isolation with geometric metrics; 2D projection and pure rotation error metrics poorly predict grasp success, success drops sharply once pose error exceeds a threshold, and a perfect pose cannot rescue grasps planned on a flawed mesh.
There is no ground truth for per-frame contact; only accumulated contact is benchmarked.
Standard single-condition metrics such as R-precision are insensitive to multi-condition hand generation; metrics for hand, body and text alignment are missing.
An evaluation bug was found in a widely used PA-MPJPE function; corrected TRACE 3DPW results are worse than reported.

Unified benchmarks covering contact, function, physics and task success are proposed but not built.
painpoints.why_it_persists: The metrics were designed for root-relative pose on static, single-agent benchmarks where ground truth exists, and measuring absolute, contact and physical correctness needs ground truth and downstream tests that are expensive to build.

painpoints.name: Camera ego-motion and sensor drift corrupt world-frame trajectories
painpoints.statement: From head-worn, hand-held or body-worn moving sensors, current methods cannot separate device motion from hand, body and object motion over long sequences, so world-frame hand trajectories drift by centimetres to decimetres, global human trajectories by metres, and portable capture devices show jumps, scale distortion and drift under fast motion, vibration and occlusion.
painpoints.description: Egocentric hand papers identify ego-motion error, not articulation, as the main source of world-space hand error (about 100 mm versus 63 mm exocentric on ACE-Data-0), and note that manipulation itself breaks the static-world assumption behind SLAM loop closure while hands leave the narrow field of view or sit at distorted fisheye edges. Global body benchmarks show GLAMR and SLAHMR drifting by metres, SLAM failing on textureless or dynamic scenes, ground-based velocity priors failing for climbing, and inertial suits drifting with time and distance even when fused with LiDAR. Portable demonstration rigs report T265 VIO jumps and scale distortion, Vive tracking interrupted by tool vibration and occlusion, headset tracking failures under fast motion, and monocular SLAM run only on stable, high-parallax clips. Device SLAM and VIO, metric-depth stages, body anchoring, gravity-aligned velocity regression, LiDAR-IMU fusion and global bundle adjustment reduce but do not remove the drift, and most of them run offline.

evidence_items.item: Egocentric hand methods have world trajectory error of about 98-102 mm, driven by ego-motion error; minutes-long takes drift.

SLAHMR diverges under fast camera motion and large focal length, DROID-SLAM fails on the textureless pitch, and global methods get relative positions between players wrong even with a shared ground plane.
T265 tracking can show sudden jumps or global scale distortion and such trajectories are auto-flagged and deleted; SLAM drift from operator anomalies leads to discarded trajectories.
Manipulation breaks the static-world assumption, so no loop closure; wrist-camera VIO occluded by hand or object fails and drifts.
Fisheye distortion at image edges degrades hand estimates and upper headset cameras often miss hands.
Localization error grows linearly with distance travelled for all methods, including the IMU plus LiDAR method.

painpoints.why_it_persists: A camera attached to the moving person sees mostly the hands and the manipulated object, which violate the static-scene assumption of odometry, while inertial integration accumulates error without absolute references. Loop closure and scene scans that bound drift are unavailable in short, cluttered, dynamic manipulation, and world-frame ground truth itself drifts (23.4 cm over 81 m on EMDB).

painpoints.name: Metric depth and placement from monocular RGB
painpoints.statement: From monocular RGB (single images, smart glasses, uncalibrated moving or internet video), hand and object estimators recover root-relative articulation but not metric depth, global translation, scale or the relative 3D placement of hand to hand and hand to object, leaving errors along the viewing ray that alignment-based metrics hide and that make the output unusable as metric action labels.
painpoints.description: Absolute hand errors are two to three times Procrustes-aligned ones, errors lie mainly along the optical axis, and several capture pipelines discard HaMeR depth as unusable; RGB-only object pose and monocular 3D point tracking trail RGB-D by a large and reportedly widening margin, and for small, far objects a 1-2 pixel scale error becomes a large depth offset. Video-to-robot data engines built on HaMeR or HaWoR plus SLAM or learned metric depth place the hand at the wrong 3D location relative to the object, which after retargeting gives missed contacts and penetration, so fine-grained hand motion is not used as supervision. Evaluation often rescales predictions with ground-truth scale or depth or reports only root-relative error, which hides the problem. Stereo, multi-view triangulation and RGB-D close much of the gap, while monocular metric-depth stages mis-scale (under on HOT3D, over on ARCTIC) and depth regularisation, bundle adjustment or stereo refinement leave residual wrist and fingertip errors of roughly 20-43 mm.

painpoints.why_it_persists: A single view does not constrain scale or depth along the viewing ray, learned monocular depth priors are inaccurate at the near range where hands operate, and the standard metrics align the error away, so the gap is neither measured nor penalized.

painpoints.name: Two hands and close bodies are confused with each other
painpoints.statement: When two hands, or two people, come close, overlap, touch or share an object, single-view and sparse-view estimators lose one of them, swap left and right or identities, misplace them relative to each other by centimetres to decimetres and produce interpenetrating meshes, so bimanual and close-contact accuracy stays well below the single-hand or single-person level.
painpoints.description: Hand and body papers describe the same failure under proximity: self-similar articulated parts overlap and occlude each other, detectors and segment trackers swap left and right hands or person identities, and pipelines such as HaMeR estimate each hand independently. Relative root placement between the two hands stays at 14-52 mm on InterHand2.6M and ARCTIC, bimanual category-agnostic reconstruction is several times worse than single-hand reconstruction, and a bimanual handover makes vision-based and VR teleoperation fail entirely. At body scale, close-contact benchmarks report errors above 50 mm, contact distances of hundreds of millimetres and wrong depth ordering, top-down detectors fail on overlapped bodies and point clouds of nearby people merge. Papers blame the lack of contact-rich training data and of joint two-agent modelling. Fixes tried are per-hand detection, two-hand tokenizers, interhand attraction and relighted synthetic data, multi-view dynamic matching, contact signatures, personalized avatars with alternating optimization and Kalman forecasting, and these need ground-truth contact, dense rigs or slow optimization.

painpoints.why_it_persists: Two hands, and two bodies, are near-identical in appearance, so identity and depth ordering are ambiguous exactly when they overlap, and most models are built and trained for one instance at a time. painpoints.name: Consumer depth is noisy, holey and device-specific at hands and objects
painpoints.statement: Commodity depth sensors (Azure Kinect ToF, RealSense structured light and stereo, iToF, iPhone LiDAR, sparse LiDAR) return noisy, quantized, missing or biased depth exactly at hands, object boundaries, fast motion and range, so RGB-D hand, body and object methods cannot rely on raw sensor depth and models trained on one sensor fail on another.
painpoints.description: Hand-object capture papers report missing values and ghost shadows at object boundaries, depth that measures skin rather than joints, iToF that is unreliable under motion, RealSense point clouds too imprecise for sim-to-real, and HO-3D sensor depth that performs worse than estimated depth. Object-pose papers find that iPhone LiDAR depth has long-tail non-Gaussian edge noise and about 0.25 m mean error, cutting ADD-S AUC by 25-40 points, that stereo and structured light are noisy beyond one metre, that NOCS lifting fails with real depth even given ground-truth NOCS maps, and that depth-input category methods collapse from 81.2 to 1.1 AP from sim to real. Body papers find point-cloud mesh recovery far worse than image HMR on real Kinect clouds, a Kinect-trained model degrading from 83 to 256 mm on iPhone LiDAR, fewer than 30 LiDAR points on a person at range, RGB-depth misalignment in fast motion, and raw RGB-D observations hurting robot policies. Where depth is clean it measurably helps (OphNet-3D, HO-3D RGB-D). Fixes tried are multi-view fusion, boundary removal, hole filling, sensor switching, synthetic noise models, noise-robust fusion networks and stereo foundation models.

evidence_items.item: Depth sensors give missing values and ghost shadows at object boundaries and become inaccurate when hands are far; single-view depth measures the skin surface, not the joint.

RGB-D 6DoF pose methods degrade sharply under depth measurement inaccuracies; iPhone LiDAR depth is low resolution with long-tail non-Gaussian noise at object edges and a mean error around 0.25 m, which impairs MegaPose's coarse module.

Point-cloud parametric recovery performs poorly on real commercial RGB-D clouds because methods depend on synthetic data (VoteHMR 144.99 mm vs image HMR 54.78 mm); Kinect-trained VoteHMR degrades to 255.71 mm on iPhone LiDAR; Kinect depth is noisy at subject boundaries.
Real HO-3D depth maps are heavily quantized with missing values, and estimated depth gave better results than sensor depth; large datasets with well-aligned depth remain scarce.
Sensor depth makes 2D-to-3D lifting inaccurate even with perfect NOCS maps; mean IoU75 drops to 22.6 percent with ground-truth NOCS.
iToF depth streams were not used because depth is unreliable under motion and phase ambiguity.

Training mostly uses synthetic or clean depth, while physically validated sensor-noise models and large real datasets with well-aligned depth are scarce.

painpoints.name: Body parts hidden by occluders, self-occlusion or truncation
painpoints.statement: When the handled object, furniture, bedding, an assistive device, another person or the wearer's own body hides much of the body, or a head-mounted, body-worn or close-range robot camera truncates limbs, single-view and sparse-view estimators cannot recover the hidden parts and fall back on priors, with errors of roughly 10 to 33 cm and near-zero detection accuracy in the worst settings.
painpoints.description: Occlusion benchmarks show monotonic degradation with severity and a large extra error when detected rather than ground-truth boxes are used; frames with scene contact are markedly worse, 2D keypoint detectors fail when objects cover the body or hands interact with them, and lifting models trained on random masks collapse once occlusion outlasts their window. Egocentric and close-range views leave lower-body and foot errors far above upper-body errors, out-of-view wrists at 12.2 cm, interaction partners truncated and blurred, and low robot cameras seeing a single limb, which ruins forecasting. From one view, motion along the optical axis and self-occluded regions (a hand hidden by the torso or reaching arm, the back of the body, the mouth interior) are unobservable and are filled by implicit-function or SMPL priors. Synthetic occlusion data, occlusion-aware lifters, masking-based training, fine-tuned detectors, stereo fisheye with scene depth, multi-camera headsets, imputation models, biomechanical model fitting and multi-frame fusion reduce but do not remove these errors, and real annotated data for practical camera placements is scarce.

painpoints.why_it_persists: The hidden parts produce no image evidence from the available viewpoint, so estimates rest on priors learned mostly from lightly occluded, full-view data, and the practical camera placements (head, robot, a single clinic camera) make missing views the normal case.

painpoints.name: Textureless, transparent, reflective, thin and small objects starve vision and depth
painpoints.statement: Objects that are textureless, transparent, specular or metallic, thin, or small and distant give too few repeatable features and invalid or biased depth, so correspondence-based pose, model-free tracking, reconstruction, segmentation and even ground-truth annotation fail on them while larger, textured, opaque objects succeed.
painpoints.description: Hand-held object papers report near-total pose failure on small objects whose visible region is mostly covered by the hand (dice ADD 2.44), depth ambiguity on thin elongated objects, noisy ToF depth on shiny, dark or metallic tools, and radiance fields, segmentation and SfM failing on transparent and reflective objects. Object-pose papers find that structured-light, stereo, ToF and LiDAR sensors miss glassware and bias depth on polished metal, that depth completion barely helps transparent-object pose, that keypoint-based SfM cannot reconstruct textureless objects (best 16.8 percent 1cm-1deg), and that for small, distant objects a 1-2 pixel scale error becomes a large depth error. Benchmarks largely avoid these objects: six of seven BOP core datasets are opaque and diffuse, and some datasets exclude reflective items from accuracy evaluation. Capture teams spray-paint, tape or mark objects, which changes their appearance, and polarization and event sensing are added as modalities without yet closing the gap.

painpoints.name: Contact location and timing cannot be inferred from images
painpoints.statement: Where and when a hand or body touches an object, the scene or another person cannot be estimated from images to the needed precision, so reconstructed contact stays centimetres off, dense contact estimators collapse out of domain, contact onset and release are rarely detected at the exact frame, and datasets rely on manual or distance-threshold labels without instantaneous contact ground truth.
painpoints.description: Bimanual and egocentric hand benchmarks report contact deviation of 3-4.5 cm, interaction-field errors of 1.5-3 cm even for challenge winners, dynamic contact mIoU near 0.2, and exact-frame contact AP of 14-24. Body papers report DECO falling to F1 0.18 out of domain, contact derived from CHORE or PHOSA reconstructions at F1 0.08-0.18, and incorrect contact prediction as the largest failure source in single-image HOI reconstruction. The causes named are that contact regions are small, self-occluded and near the image resolution limit, that small pose errors produce penetration or floating, that MANO and SMPL surfaces misalign with real skin, and that proximity cannot be told from force-transmitting contact. Threshold labels inherit pose and scan errors and teach models to predict contact almost everywhere. Measured contact (MIDI keyboards, wet paint, tactile gloves, pressure insoles) exists only in special setups, often only as accumulated contact.

evidence_items.item: Egocentric ARCTIC contact deviation stays at 32.56 mm for the best entry; contact remains centimetres off.

Geometry-based contact from current 3D human and object reconstruction is very poor (CHORE F1 0.08, PHOSA F1 0.18), and DECO itself reaches only F1 0.18 with 44-46 cm geodesic error out of domain on BEHAVE.

Absolute contact accuracy remains low even for the best method; real-world datasets lack contact ground truth, the benchmark has only accumulated contact, and MANO annotations misalign with real hands.
Existing contact methods lack the temporal granularity to find contact onset; near-touch frames are ambiguous under ego-motion, occlusion and motion blur.
Spatial priors cannot tell whether proximity is real, force-transmitting contact; geometric metrics do not establish correct contact.
False negatives at grasp initiation and hallucinated lingering pressure at release arise from egocentric self-occlusion of the hand-object gap.

painpoints.why_it_persists: Contact is a millimetre-scale relation between two surfaces that occlude each other at the moment it happens, so the image carries almost no direct evidence, and no sensor gives per-frame contact ground truth on arbitrary objects without instrumenting them. Methods therefore learn from derived labels whose errors are as large as the quantity being measured.

painpoints.name: Articulated and deformable handled objects
painpoints.statement: Objects whose shape changes during manipulation, articulated parts and deformables, cannot be captured, tracked, reconstructed or simulated with the hands at the fidelity available for rigid objects, because datasets treat them as rigid or single-DoF, every tested tracker nearly fails on movable parts, and there is no common pose definition, canonical pose or metric for them.
painpoints.description: Hand-object papers report that automatic tracking of articulated and non-rigid objects is unsolved, that articulation priors are category-specific and depth-dependent and fail with clutter, hands and noisy monocular depth, and that deformable reconstruction needs pre-scanned templates, uniform material and ten synchronized cameras while covering only small deformations. Object-pose papers measure the drop directly: model-based tracking on PACE falls from 38.1 to 10.1 ADD(-S) AUC from rigid to articulated objects and category-level AP falls to about 1, while HANDAL treats articulated tools as rigid in a default state and deformable boxes break annotation. Surveys state that deformable and articulated objects lack common pose definitions and metrics, and robot simulators lack stable deformable physics. Fixes tried are category articulation priors with depth, deformation graphs over templates, part-wise scans and PBD or FEM simulation, and none generalizes to novel categories or monocular input.

evidence_items.item: Fully automatic tracking of articulated and non-rigid objects is not solved; non-rigid objects get only segmentation masks.

Current articulation methods are too dependent on accurate depth or fail in the presence of clutter and hands.
Monocular hand-object reconstruction fails on hand-deformable object interaction; the dataset holds only small deformations and the method needs uniform material.
PBD garment simulation is unstable and FEM does not capture garment deformation; grasps fail on occluded or heavily deformed regions.
Cannot generalize to novel categories because articulation priors are object-specific; relies more on depth than texture.

painpoints.attempted_fixes: Category articulation priors with depth (ContactArt), deformation graphs over scanned templates with dense views (HMDO), part-wise scans, synthetic-only articulation models (CAPTRA, ANCSH; 4.4 percent on PACE articulated), treating articulated objects as rigid in a default state, and PBD or FEM simulation. Formal pose definitions and metrics are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Articulation and deformation add unknown degrees of freedom on top of the unknown object shape and the occlusion by the hand, while annotation tools, metrics and simulators are built around a single rigid 6D pose, so neither labels nor evaluation exist for the general case.

painpoints.name: Finger pose of the grasping hand under occlusion
painpoints.statement: From a single RGB or RGB-D view, an egocentric headset or a few ad-hoc cameras, the field cannot recover finger-level 3D pose of a hand that is grasping or manipulating an object: errors concentrate at the thumb and fingertips, rise sharply with object and self-occlusion, heavily occluded hands are dropped, and reliable finger kinematics still require a large calibrated multi-camera space.
painpoints.description: Hand mesh and keypoint failures concentrate in object occlusion and self-occlusion; the thumb and fingertips carry the largest errors and accuracy collapses beyond roughly 80 percent hand coverage. Headset trackers (UmeTrack, consumer VR SDKs) lose track during grasps, detectors miss heavily occluded hands, and even dense-dome and marker annotation degrades during interaction compared with free-hand motion. The same holds in clinical rooms: three webcams around an assessment table exceed the laboratory reprojection standard and give no reliable finger kinematics, and usable finger-tapping capture needed six synchronized cameras in a large room. The causes named are the small visible hand area, the ambiguity of hidden joints and harder 2D-to-3D lifting when the object covers the hand. New backbones, diffusion hypotheses, IMU or EMG fusion, synthetic data and fine-tuning on occluded frames each give small gains, interpolation across missing frames accumulates error, and multi-view input helps only with calibrated rigs that do not transfer across layouts.

painpoints.settings: Monocular RGB single-hand crops (DexYCB, HO3D v2, with FreiHAND for contrast); egocentric headset monochrome or stereo (HOT3D, UmeTrack, AssemblyHands, HandSense, DexGloveHOI, Apple Vision Pro, Quest); Ego-Exo4D; exocentric kitchen and home captures; surgical egocentric RGB-D (POV-Surgery); bimanual monocular video (ARCTIC); clinical rooms with one to three ad-hoc cameras or six synchronized cameras (TULIP finger tapping, stroke ARAT grasp tasks, monocular reachable workspace).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: New backbones (sub-millimetre gains); probabilistic diffusion hypotheses (best-of-N selection needs ground truth and is slower); IMU gloves and EMG wristbands (change hand appearance or fail across users); large synthetic RGB-D data (2-3 percent); fine-tuning on occluded frames; linear interpolation or discarding of low-confidence frames (error accumulates over consecutive gaps); calibrated multi-view rigs (do not generalize across layouts); in the clinic, off-the-shelf MediaPipe/MMPose keypoints triangulated with outlier interpolation and smoothing, biomechanical model fitting, and proposed five-camera or small-room hardware that is untested.
painpoints.why_it_persists: The hidden joints produce no image evidence, so a single view must infer them from priors, the training labels that would teach those priors are least accurate exactly during grasps, and adding views needs calibrated rigs that wearables and clinics do not have.

painpoints.name: Whole-body capture loses the hands and the handled object
painpoints.statement: When the whole body is captured (consumer RGB-D rigs, body mocap, full-body domes, sparse VR trackers, monocular or egocentric video), finger articulation, the wrist anchor and the handled object are not recovered at the fidelity of dedicated hand capture: wrists and lower-arm rotations carry the largest body errors, hands jitter, interpenetrate or are omitted, and scaled human capture excludes object interaction by design.
painpoints.description: Body-scale capture leaves the hand at low resolution: Kinect depth is too noisy for fingers, body marker sets do not track most finger articulation, full-body domes lack pixel density on hands and faces, and Gaussian methods leave too few primitives there. Per-joint breakdowns show wrists, ankles and lower-arm rotations with the highest errors even when visible, and much higher out of view, while the wrist anchors any hand-object reconstruction built on a body estimate. Datasets therefore paste unrelated GRAB or ARCTIC hand motion onto bodies, capture hands in separate sessions without objects, restrict subjects to no object interaction in order to scale, or track only arm kinematics in clinical grasp tasks. Downstream, hand-position errors propagate to the full body (MPJPE 12.42 cm with predicted hands versus 7.01 cm with ground-truth hands), and humanoid or robot policies built on such data fail on hand-precision tasks. External hand trackers, wrist-only markers, glove-aware fitting, hardcase mining, separate high-density hand captures and manual landmark correction leave hands and objects outside the joint capture.

painpoints.why_it_persists: A camera framing the whole body gives the hand few pixels and a body model gives it few degrees of freedom, while scaled human capture drops object interaction to stay tractable, so no dataset or model covers body, fingers and object together.

painpoints.name: Single-hand, single-object, single-agent scope
painpoints.statement: Most hand-object datasets, methods and human-to-robot pipelines assume one, usually right, hand interacting with one rigid object by one demonstrator without body or scene context, so bimanual cooperation, handovers, multi-object and multi-person interaction and joint hand-body-object estimation remain largely uncovered and, where they are tested, perform worst.
painpoints.description: Dataset and method papers list two-handed manipulation, bimanual pressure and bimanual grasp generation as future work, and one states that single-hand manipulation itself is not yet solved. Datasets are fragmented: full-body sets lack hands, hand sets lack body and global context, and modalities are split across short clips. In robot learning, transfer is restricted to the right hand, to single-hand to single-gripper mappings or to single-arm grippers, and bimanual tasks such as pot-lifting and cloth folding are the hardest and degrade more out of distribution. The human-video survey states that nearly all methods assume one demonstrator and one robot, and that multi-agent settings need agent correspondence, disentangled overlapping motions and contact tracking across shared objects, which current pipelines do not do. Newer bimanual and multi-person datasets and dual-arm UMI-style collection extend coverage but stay in instrumented labs with few subjects, objects and sites.

painpoints.settings: Single-hand datasets and baselines (HOI4D, HOGraspNet, EgoPressure, HUG, DexYCB, HO3D); multi-person handover (HOH, CORE4D, ADL4D); body-hand activity datasets (EPFL-Smart-Kitchen, AssemblyHands-X, Ego-Exo4D, ParaHome); human-to-robot transfer to single-arm grippers and dexterous hands; bimanual mobile manipulators (EgoVerse), simulated twins (RoboTube) and handheld bimanual grippers (UMI, FastUMI).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: New bimanual and multi-person datasets (ARCTIC, OakInk2, GigaHands, HOH, CORE4D), integrated ego-exo body-hand-object capture (ACE-Data-0, ParaHome, HUMOTO), dual-arm UMI-style collection and co-training with aligned bimanual robot data. All rely on lab rigs with few people, objects or sites, and no method handles two-hand or multi-agent correspondence with shared-object contact.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Every additional hand, object or agent multiplies occlusion, annotation effort and the correspondence problem, so dataset builders and method designers restrict scope to keep capture and modelling tractable. The gap is circular: bimanual data are scarce because bimanual tracking is unreliable, and bimanual tracking is unreliable because accurately labelled bimanual data are scarce.

painpoints.name: Reconstructed and generated interactions are not physically consistent
painpoints.statement: Kinematic reconstruction, multi-object scene reconstruction, interaction generation and learned world models do not enforce contact, gravity, support or non-penetration, so their outputs show interpenetration, floating objects, hovering hands, foot sliding and contact without force, and the mocap interaction datasets used for training carry the same artifacts.
painpoints.description: Body-object papers see penetration, floating and jitter in monocular, egocentric and sparse-signal pose output, in interaction generators, and in the training data itself, where InterAct finds penetration, floating contacts, inaccurate hands and jitter across seven mocap HOI datasets. Single-image multi-object reconstruction treats objects independently and leaves inter-object penetration and floating poses with object IoU below 0.45, and pose surveys list scene-level physical consistency as open. Robot-learning surveys and a position paper state that world models trained on human video optimise visual similarity, so rollouts show interpenetration, contact without force and deforming rigid objects, and users spot generated videos by physics and contact cues. Fixes tried are guidance losses, which add jitter, occupancy and contact-correction terms, which fail on large errors, intuitive-physics terms limited to one flat floor and static poses, post-hoc penetration removal, pressure sensing confined to a mat, and physics simulators, which are action-specific and fit poorly with diffusion models.

evidence_items.item: SAM 3D treats objects independently, giving inter-object penetrations and unstable floating poses; absolute object-level IoU stays below 0.45 on all four benchmarks; prior benchmarks have inaccurate registration and penetrations.
MoCap HOI data carry penetration, floating contacts, inaccurate hand poses and jitter; correction fails on severe source noise, and physics imitation succeeds 84.4% on raw vs 90.7% on corrected data.

Purely learned predictors produce futures where objects interpenetrate, contacts occur without force, or rigid objects deform; 3D representations may struggle with contact, force and material response, and mechanics-based models are brittle when the environment is unknown or deformable.

Image-based body estimates lean, hover and penetrate the ground; the intuitive-physics terms handle only body-floor contact on a single flat plane, break on multiple or inconsistent ground planes, and target static poses.
Generated interactions lack physical plausibility in gravity and force interaction; physics-simulator methods are action-specific, generalize poorly and fit poorly with diffusion models.
Generated HOI states ignore gravity (a keyboard floats without contact), and interpenetration persists when actions conflict with objects.

painpoints.why_it_persists: The dominant representations (independent per-object meshes, kinematic skeletons, pixels) carry no mass, support or contact force, and adding physics needs object mass, friction and contact state that are not observed. Differentiable or simulated physics is slow, task-specific and brittle under the noisy kinematic input it would have to correct.

painpoints.name: Scaled in-the-wild data rests on unverified pseudo-labels and filtering
painpoints.statement: Large egocentric, internet and multi-view human datasets label hands, bodies, depth and geometry with monocular estimators, headset trackers or foundation models whose accuracy on the released data cannot be measured, and their pipelines discard the occluded, blurred and truncated frames where those labels fail, so the data that scales has unverified labels and is biased toward easy views.
painpoints.description: Hand and robot-learning datasets state that their 3D hand labels are predictions from HaMeR, HaWoR, MediaPipe, ARKit, Aria MPS or VR SDKs that are off by centimetres under occlusion and fast motion, and that quality is checked only by reprojection consistency, qualitative overlay, cross-dataset consistency or VLA validation loss; one finds that its unverified variant gives little gain over no pretraining. Avatar and body datasets similarly substitute Sapiens normals, rendered depth, off-the-shelf mask and SMPL fits and pseudo-ground-truth trajectories for measured geometry outside the lab. Video-to-robot pipelines retain only 6.9 to 17.3 percent of EPIC-Kitchens and Ego4D frames and reject a third of lab-video candidates, mostly where reconstruction or retargeting fails. Downstream effects are measurable: action accuracy and grasp oracles drop with tracking error, and some pose labels are judged too inaccurate to train pose estimators. Multi-view re-annotation of subsets and calibration-room checks are the only quantitative validation reported.

painpoints.name: Jitter, drift and unrecoverable track loss over time
painpoints.statement: Per-frame and short-window estimators and 6D object trackers cannot maintain a stable, continuous track of people, limbs and objects over long sequences: outputs jitter, trackers drift and cannot re-acquire an object once lost, interpolation collapses when occlusion outlasts the model window, and identities switch when bodies overlap or the camera moves fast.
painpoints.description: Body and hand estimators jitter most in heavily occluded frames and for hands, monocular video methods jitter even with ground-truth boxes, and interpolation-based lifters collapse to about 302 mm when occlusion exceeds their 81-frame window. Model-free object trackers such as BundleTrack cannot recover once they lose the object, propagating the previous pose fails under large inter-frame displacement, point-tracking relative poses drift over long sequences, and FoundationPose fails under simultaneous camera and object motion. Mask and point trackers lose thin or textureless parts and must be re-initialised, and person trackers switch identities under overlap, rapid egocentric motion or low light. Evaluation hides much of this: BOP scores per image, tracking benchmarks initialise from a perturbed ground-truth pose, and no dedicated short-term object tracking metric exists. Motion priors, forecasting for occluded keypoints, periodic re-initialisation, EKF/RTS smoothing and longer windows reduce jitter and drift but do not remove them.

evidence_items.item: Model-free trackers cannot recover once the object is lost (BundleTrack); robust tracking in clutter and occlusion with recovery after loss is open.
Per-frame separate fitting yields jitter; residual jitter from detector sensitivity to occlusion and inter-camera delays remains and is worse for hands; advanced motion priors are future work.
The original DTF collapses to about 302 mm MPJPE when occlusion outlasts its 81-frame interpolation window; interpolation-based occlusion handling fails for prolonged occlusion.
Frame-based methods cannot maintain identity assignments and coherent trajectories when bodies overlap or exchange positions; temporal reasoning for identity-consistent motion is future work.
Prior trackers suffer person-ID switches from rapid camera motion, occlusion and unconstrained activity; the proposed method still reports 741 ID switches.
Direct temporal propagation of the previous pose fails with large inter-frame displacement in fast motion, and fusion propagation gives poor initial poses that the current frame cannot correct.

EgoHumans / 741 ID switches remain after a 13.6% IDF1 gain [1248]
EHPT-XC / IDF1 at most 22.72; best MOTA 47.37 [432]

painpoints.settings: Multi-Kinect HOI capture (InterCap, COUCH); monocular HOI video (RHOBIN); moving hand-held cameras (EMDB); occlusion lifting (BlendMimic3D); multi-person RGB-D groups and egocentric multi-human tracking (HUM4D, EgoHumans, Harmony4D); low-light multi-person tracking (EHPT-XC); clinical prosthesis video (ProGait, RSP3D); moving-object tracking in RGB-D and RGB (PACE, Omni6DPose ROPE, DynOPETs, EgoXtreme, OmniPose6D on HO3D/YCBInEOAT/DexYCB, DTTD-Mobile); per-image evaluation in BOP.

painpoints.name: Estimators fail outside their training capture domain
painpoints.statement: Hand, hand-object and human reconstruction models trained on one lab dataset, subject pool, camera rig, headset layout or object-centric corpus lose a large share of their accuracy on another dataset, in-the-wild scenes, new headset extrinsics, unseen views and interaction patterns, specialised domains such as surgery, or on humans, with errors growing from about 1.5x to several-fold until target-domain data is added.
painpoints.description: Cross-dataset tests between lab hand benchmarks (DexYCB, TACO, HOGraspNet, HO3D, OakInk, ADL4D) double or triple errors, studio-trained headset trackers regress in the wild and collapse on another headset layout (184.27 mm on HOT3D without extrinsic augmentation), pressure estimators fail on unseen views, and surgical and fingerspelling domains show the same effect. Generalizable human NeRFs trained on MVHumanNet show a domain gap on HuMMan until fine-tuned, generalized NeRFs degrade on handheld camera-pose configurations, and point-map, large-reconstruction and inverse-rendering models that work on objects degrade on humans without human training data. Papers attribute the gap to dataset bias imposed by the capture and annotation method, monotonous lab appearance, markers, and limited subjects, scenes and camera layouts. Joint multi-dataset training, extrinsic augmentation, in-the-wild contrastive pretraining and target fine-tuning narrow but do not remove the gap.

painpoints.why_it_persists: Each capture rig fixes its viewpoints, backgrounds, subjects and annotation errors, models learn those regularities, and no dataset spans the conditions of deployment, so target-domain labels remain the missing ingredient.

painpoints.name: Fast motion, motion blur and low light break RGB capture
painpoints.statement: Under fast or high-acceleration motion, motion blur, low frame rates and dark, extreme or smoky lighting, RGB and RGB-D detection, pose estimation and the ground-truth pipelines behind them degrade strongly, image restoration does not help, and event cameras that tolerate these conditions lack established pose algorithms and accurate labels.
painpoints.description: Body papers show models trained on Human3.6M failing on athletic motion (ankle errors up to 560 mm, lower-limb velocity correlation 0.11), optimisation methods oversmoothing fast motion, 10 fps LiDAR and robot cameras missing fast limbs, and HOI capture avoiding very fast interactions because of blur and RGB-depth misalignment. Hand recovery under real blur is temporally ambiguous, deblurring first does not work, and real blurred datasets with 3D ground truth are rare because annotation on degraded frames is unreliable. Object-pose papers show zero-shot RGB estimators collapsing under fast egocentric sports motion, smoke and extreme light, deblurring, dehazing and low-light enhancement lowering recall further, and no established pose algorithm on event data. Dataset builders avoid the condition with stop-and-go capture, fixed lighting or blur filtering, and event fusion, beam-splitter rigs and domain fine-tuning help only in narrow settings.

evidence_items.item: RGB-only zero-shot estimators (FoundPose, GigaPose, PicoPose) degrade strongly under extreme lighting and smoke; deblur, dehaze and low-light enhancement do not help and often hurt; FoundPose often fails to get the minimum correspondences for PnP-RANSAC under cropping and blur.
Models trained on Human3.6M fail on athletic motion (MPJPE 234-257 mm, ankle up to 560 mm); lower-limb velocity correlation is only r=0.11.
3D hand methods disregard motion blur; a blurry image is temporally ambiguous, deblurring first does not work, and event-only input fails on static hands.
Very fast interactions were avoided because of motion blur and RGB-depth misalignment limits of the sensor.
SLAHMR produces overly smooth motion, missing fast movements; fast motion and low player resolution degrade 2D detectors.
RGB-only methods misinterpret low-light plus heavy-blur scenes, giving missed and false-positive persons; annotating poses directly on degraded frames is unreliable.

painpoints.settings: Sports and martial arts (AthletePose3D, RELI11D, HardMo, WorldPose), blurred hands with events (EBH), low-light tracking (EHPT-XC), pre-collision pedestrians (PVCP), Kinect HOI capture (InterCap), 10 fps LiDAR (LIP), robot-view forecasting (HARPER); egocentric Aria in sports, smoke and maintenance (EgoXtreme), event plus RGB-D (YCB-Ev), dark long-range Kinect (DTTD), glare in handheld capture (HANDAL).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Event-RGB fusion, beam-splitter rigs for sharp references, synthetic blur (domain gap), domain fine-tuning, hardcase pseudo-labels, deblurring, dehazing and low-light enhancement (which lower recall), temporal propagation (fails under large displacement), stop-and-go capture, fixed lighting and blur filtering. Pose estimation directly on events is proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Exposure time and frame rate of commodity cameras integrate fast hand and tool motion into blur, and the same degradation corrupts the labelling pipelines, so the hardest frames have neither clean evidence nor ground truth. Event sensors avoid blur but need new algorithms and synchronized ground truth that do not exist yet.

painpoints.name: Embodiment gap: human hand motion does not map to executable robot actions
painpoints.statement: Human hand and body demonstrations cannot yet be turned reliably into executable robot or humanoid actions, because kinematic retargeting yields self-collision, joint-limit violations and floating or penetrating fingers, functional correspondence across hand morphologies is undefined, human strategies and workspaces do not suit the robot, and bimanual transfer performs worst.
painpoints.description: Robot-learning and hand papers report that kinematic IK without contact terms leaves almost half of audited trajectories with non-grasp self-contact, that retargeting causes most rejected samples in a human-to-robot editing benchmark, that seed-level kinematic retargeting on an Allegro hand succeeds about 1 percent of the time, and that trajectory-centric transfer reaches goals by air grasps or penetration because contact and force are ignored. Even in simulation with mocap references, bimanual tracking succeeds about half the time versus three quarters for single-hand tasks, humanoid pipelines reach about 5 percent on box lifting, and retail VLA tasks fail on finger shaping around small packages. Beyond reconstruction error, the human strategy itself can be wrong for the robot (two hands versus one gripper, human-ergonomic sanding directions, workspace limits), and mappings are tied to one robot hand. Residual policies, contact-map transfer, per-hand mapping matrices, learned hand-to-gripper transfer and per-object RL are tried, and task-preserving retargeting that keeps contact and object-state transitions is proposed.

evidence_items.item: Trajectory-centric transfer ignores contact formation; the kinematic baseline achieves goals via air grasping or mesh penetration.
The best pipeline reaches only 6/5 percent success on box lifting; copy-rotation and OmniH2O retargeting fail (0 percent) on hand-precision tasks; the humanoid has no dexterous hands.

Kinematic retargeting models neither self-collision nor physical contact; only 55.2% of audited trajectories were free of non-grasp self-contact and 62.5% free of joint-limit violation, so outputs are not executable demonstrations.

On bag-grocery, Robot B performance dropped with human co-training because its demonstrations used one gripper to prop the bag open, unlike the two-handed human strategy; embodiment factors need deeper analysis.
Human and robot grasps are paired only semantically; functional equivalence across morphologies is undefined; kinematic retargeting gives low success.
Large performance gap between single-hand and bimanual tasks when transferring mocap to dexterous hands; the framework lacks a bimanual coordination design.

painpoints.attempted_fixes: Residual mixture-of-experts policies, contact-map transfer, unified state spaces, VLA pretraining on reconstructed hands, per-object RL, tactile-aware rewards, depth and physics refinement, joint-limit clamping, per-hand mapping matrices, learned hand-to-gripper transfer, optimization-based retargeting and human screening. Task-preserving retargeting is proposed but not built.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Human and robot hands differ in size, kinematics, actuation and contact mechanics, so no pose-level correspondence preserves the effect on the object, and the contact and force information that effect-level retargeting would need is missing from human data.

painpoints.name: Interaction forecasting and synthesis do not generalize
painpoints.statement: Models that forecast or generate hand-object, human-object and human-human interaction lose accuracy within one to three seconds, degrade on unseen objects, tasks and populations, often produce invalid contact, and cannot plan long multi-step manipulation end to end, because they are trained on small, mostly single-person, single-object mocap sets.
painpoints.description: Hand benchmarks show forecasting errors of several centimetres and tens of degrees that grow with horizon and with novel tools, objects and subjects, generative forecasters worse than predictive ones, anticipation near floor under head motion, and LLM primitive planning failing beyond five primitives. Body-object papers report generators producing intersections for actions outside the training set, misaligned dual-branch human and object generation, contact degrading on unseen objects and chair shapes, and coupled two-person prediction degrading on an unseen task. Forecasting from robot-estimated partial poses is several times worse than from ground truth, so forecasting inherits perception error. Fixes tried are text, gaze and intention conditioning, contact and penetration guidance, physics post-processing, dataset aggregation and correction, and model scaling, which saturates.

evidence_items.item: Forecasting errors rise for the right hand and tool under novel geometries; generative forecasters have far larger errors; grasp synthesis has more collisions on unseen tool geometries.
The motion generator cannot produce human-object interactions outside the training distribution; climbing off a table yields unrealistic motion and object intersections.
LLM primitive planning succeeds only 36 percent overall and fails for tasks with more than five primitives; no end-to-end text-to-manipulation framework exists.
Forecasting baselines degrade on unseen object shapes; interaction synthesis produces inter-penetration and unnatural contact.
Naive dual-branch generation misaligns human and object motions, and conditioning human motion on generated object motion causes a large performance drop.
Trajectory prediction error grows with horizon, from 0.031 m at 1 s to 0.053 m at 3 s.

painpoints.why_it_persists: Interaction data are costly to capture and therefore small and narrow, while the space of objects and tasks is open, so generative models interpolate within the training set; physical validity and perception noise are not modelled during training.

painpoints.name: Benchmarks are saturated, fragmented or unvalidated for real use
painpoints.statement: Standard benchmarks are near saturation on controlled scenes, fragmented across robots, rigs and protocols, or not validated against the target use, so methods that rank well hide large real-world drops and results cannot be compared or attributed.
painpoints.description: Object-pose papers call household benchmarks near saturation and show methods losing large margins on industrial bins, longer range, dynamic, egocentric or rearranged scenes, while standard sets contain opaque objects on one support plane with static cameras; each new dataset covers one gap and several stay small. Robot-learning papers report evaluation fragmented across robots, tasks and video sources, real-robot results confounded by hardware, camera placement and reset noise, many datasets validated only by offline losses or visual metrics, and success-only scores that do not locate the failing component. Avatar and clinical papers report missing shared benchmarks and protocols, comparisons at downscaled resolution, intermediate metrics such as trajectory accuracy that do not predict downstream quality, and clinical scores built on small or healthy-only cohorts, subjective reference labels with very low inter-rater agreement and borrowed minimal clinically important differences. Standardised hardware and protocols, simulated twins, diagnostic metrics and new targeted datasets are the responses so far.

evidence_items.item: Household 6D benchmarks are near saturation and do not reflect industrial complexity.
Trajectory accuracy does not translate directly into downstream reconstruction and synthesis quality; investigating why is future work.
Benchmarking is fragmented across robots, tasks and video sources, and most methods cannot be benchmarked in simulation alone, so which transfer choices cause better performance remains unclear.

Clinician agreement on kinetic tremor is very low (ICC 0.1 right, 0.4 left), limiting label reliability; the best finger-tapping model is commensurate only with the least accurate clinician; the cohort is small relative to PD heterogeneity with low demographic diversity; a deep pose-sequence classifier underperformed due to small dataset size.
Poor real-world performance is hidden by constrained benchmarks such as NOCS-REAL275 (six categories, 18 videos).
Standard datasets contain opaque, diffuse, hand-sized objects on a single support plane, centred in view; realistic benchmarks with natural clutter, backgrounds and material variety are needed.

benchmark_evidence: XYZ-IBD / unseen-object 6D detection AP: best SAM6D 0.578, FoundationPose 0.564, versus 0.70-0.73 on BOP-Core5 (402)
UMI-Bench 1.0 overall (1372) / overall score: best model averages 55.84 of 100 across ten tasks.

painpoints.settings: BOP core, REAL275, YCB-Video and LINEMOD versus industrial, clutter, long-range, mobile, event, egocentric and dynamic sets (XYZ-IBD, PACE, DTTD, EgoXtreme, DynOPETs, YCB-Ev); real-robot evaluation across labs (UMI-Bench), offline-validated egocentric datasets, simulated twins, MLLM judges; head NVS (RenderMe-360, NeRSemble), ActorsHQ, SmartPortraits; Parkinson's UPDRS scoring (TULIP), stroke ARAT and reachable-workspace scoring.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: New targeted datasets, standardised UMI hardware with released protocols and rollout audits, simulated twins, diagnostic H2R metrics, fixed NVS and clinical protocols and leave-one-subject-out evaluation. 3DGS benchmark scenes, component-level credit assignment, prospective clinical cohorts and measure-specific MCIDs are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Benchmark construction follows what is cheap to annotate, which is controlled static capture, and real-world evaluation needs physical robots, patients or field capture that differ between labs, so shared, validated, task-linked protocols are costly and rarely funded.

painpoints.name: Contact force is unobservable from vision and unmeasured in natural capture
painpoints.statement: Hand-object contact force, pressure, ground and object reaction forces, joint torques and muscle activity cannot be measured during natural manipulation without instrumenting the hand, object or floor and cannot be inferred from video outside the lab, so human demonstration and video datasets carry no measured force and vision-to-force models collapse on unseen views, tasks and scenes.
painpoints.description: Hand papers call force the causal signal of manipulation yet note that it cannot be labelled manually and is absent from video datasets; pressure pads are flat, tactile gloves are uncomfortable, drift, miss small parts and change hand appearance, and vision-to-pressure models lose about half their contact IoU on unseen views or interaction patterns. Body papers report that dynamics ground truth needs force plates, pressure mats, insoles or EMG confined to labs, that simulation datasets model only ground reaction forces or assume weightless objects, and that force-from-motion models are not real-time or not validated. Robot-learning papers state that human demonstration datasets omit tactile and force signals, that the available tactile labels are binary mesh-distance contact, that simulation benchmarks substitute proprioception for touch, and that no hand-held powered tool with integrated force sensing exists because the sensor would impair ergonomics. Inferred or pseudo-tactile cues and full-hand tactile sensing are listed as future work.

evidence_items.item: Force is absent from egocentric datasets because it cannot be manually labelled; glove sensors are uncomfortable, unreliable over time and interfere with fine manipulation.
External force measurement outside mocap labs is unreliable; force-from-motion models are not real-time or not validated, and out-of-distribution multi-activity models exceed 25% body-weight error.

Tactile datasets remain small and narrow in contact coverage; HOI-Tac tactile labels are binary per-vertex contact from hand-object mesh distance thresholding, not measured force; human demonstration datasets largely omit the tactile modality.
Pressure sensing is confined to flat surfaces; arbitrary object surfaces would need hand instrumentation that hinders natural interaction.
Occlusion breaks pixel-to-pressure alignment in egocentric grasping; RGB models fail on rare interaction patterns without explicit hand and object pose.
Force estimation from observation alone is under-constrained; sensors alter contact mechanics; forces are derived from physics simulation, not measured.

benchmark_evidence: EgoPressure unseen exocentric views / contact IoU 36.82 percent vs 62.11 percent on seen views (98)
AddBiomechanics / GRF error best 1.17 N/kg, joint torque 1.33 Nm/kg; only 21.2% of data clinical-grade [334]
Real robot PlugIn with visual defects (1385) / success rate: 20 percent (gripper) and 10 percent (DexBotic) in-distribution, 20 percent out-of-distribution; all baselines 0 percent.

painpoints.settings: Egocentric RGB with a pressure pad (EgoPressure); tactile gloves (EgoTactile, HT-Bench, TactiDex, HRDexDB); force-tactile gripper on furniture (Hoi!); force plates with mocap (AddBiomechanics); simulated humanoids and musculoskeletal models (ImDy, MinT); pressure mats and insoles (MoYo, MMVP); sEMG; human video and glove datasets for VLA pretraining, contact-rich robot tasks and hand-held tool use.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Pressure pads, tactile gloves, glove-to-bare-hand translation, force-supervised pretraining, simulation-derived forces, musculoskeletal simulation, pressure-RGB fusion, diffusion pressure models (2.8 FPS with flicker), mesh-distance contact labels, simulated tactile on MANO, haptic teleoperation and fixtured force-torque sensors. Wrist EMG, pose-conditioned pressure and pseudo-tactile cues are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Force is not visible: it depends on mass, friction and stiffness that images do not show, and every sensor that measures it sits at the contact interface, where it changes the interaction. Vision-to-force learning therefore has only small, lab-bound paired data.

painpoints.name: Fine-grained actions, phases and events cannot be inferred automatically
painpoints.statement: Video and vision-language models cannot reliably recognise fine-grained hand-object actions, simultaneous two-handed actions, grasp and release stages, contact events, object-state changes, mistakes and task completion from unscripted manipulation video, nor reason about 3D hand and object kinematics, so pipelines rely on human labelling and verification.
painpoints.description: Egocentric benchmarks report verb recognition far below noun recognition, roughly half accuracy for cross-view and simultaneous two-handed actions, near-floor state-change detection, and VLMs answering 3D, object-motion and kinematics questions at 20-35 percent versus over 90 percent for humans. Action segmentation learns action order rather than the current action, and recognition from predicted hand poses is worse than from annotated poses, which ties the gap to pose quality. Robot-learning datasets report that VLM-generated atomic-action labels hallucinate and need human-in-the-loop correction, that VLM completion verification is near chance, and that no temporal segmentation method meets their needs. The position paper names automatic alignment of video, mocap, tactile and robot logs to a common event timeline, with joint inference of phase, contact and object state, as the missing mechanism. Hard-negative contrastive training, hand plus body pose input and gaze fusion help only partly.

evidence_items.item: EgoVLMs fail to choose the correct caption among single-word substitutions; verb accuracy is much lower than noun accuracy due to object-centric feature spaces.
Model hallucinations in atomic-action labels require human-in-the-loop correction, and passive video lacks action boundaries.
Recognizing simultaneous, overlapping fine-grained actions of both hands is open; accuracy on the view split is roughly half that on the person split.
Models confuse left/right directions and fixtures in 3D and object-motion questions; Gemini Pro reaches 20.8 percent on object motion.
Action recognition from predicted hand poses is lower than from annotated poses, showing pose quality matters.

Multimodal streams (video, mocap, tactile, logs) are asynchronous and aligning them to physical events is itself unsolved; inferring events, contacts and object states from partially supervised episodes is open.

WIYH human-centric vision-language benchmark (1376) / completion verification: only slightly above 50 percent random for all VLMs.
HD-EPIC VQA / Gemini Pro 3D perception 32.5 and object motion 20.8 percent vs human 93.8 and 92.7 (1398)
HoloAssist (1397) / fine-grained action recognition top-1: around 35 percent (coarse around 50 percent).
ATTACH / view-split recognition 33.2 percent vs 57.4 percent person split (1189)
painpoints.settings: Egocentric video (Ego4D, EPIC, HD-EPIC, Assembly101, IndEgo, HOI4D, AssemblyHands, EPFL-Smart-Kitchen), multi-Kinect assembly (ATTACH), ADL4D, Ego-Exo4D, ChildPlay-Hand, handover failure video (HFD), TACO; unscripted egocentric video captioned by VLMs (WIYH, Open-AoE, HumanNet, EgoLive), HoloAssist, EgoExoLearn, multimodal capture with mocap, tactile and robot logs.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Hard-negative contrastive objectives (EgoNCE++), hand plus body pose input, multi-view and gaze fusion (which can hurt), fine-tuned small VLMs, temporal action models, VLM labels with human verification and fixed-interval segmentation. Embodied autolabelling and failure-centric datasets are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Video and language models are trained with object-centric, caption-level supervision that carries no 3D hand and object state, so verbs and contact events, which are defined by small 3D changes, are under-determined, and event-level ground truth is labour-intensive and partly subjective.

painpoints.name: Novel objects in dense clutter
painpoints.statement: Two-stage 6D pose pipelines cannot reliably detect, segment and pose novel objects in dense real clutter (piles, bins, cluttered tabletops), because unseen-object detection trails seen-object detection by tens of AP points and every method family loses pose accuracy steeply as the visible fraction shrinks, while many benchmarks hide the detection stage by supplying ground-truth masks or boxes.
painpoints.description: BOP 2023 and 2024 name 2D detection of unseen objects as the main 6D pipeline bottleneck, lagging seen-object detection by about 35 percent, and zero-shot proposal generators built on SAM or FastSAM and open-vocabulary segmenters lose much of their accuracy on industrial bins, dense piles and cluttered desktops and assign wrong IDs among stacked identical parts. Pose accuracy falls steadily with occlusion (MegaPose 77.9 to 42.3 ADD(-S) from low to high occlusion), and in PACE clutter learned instance-level networks fall below classical point-pair matching even with ground-truth detections. Surveys state that no method handles severe occlusion, that occlusion-specific methods do not beat general ones and that occlusion patterns have not been studied systematically. Many dataset and method papers supply ground-truth boxes or masks, so reported pose numbers leave out detection error, and new clutter datasets document the drop without fixing it.

evidence_items.item: 2D detection of unseen objects is the main bottleneck of 6D pipelines and lags seen-object detection by about 35%.
All pose methods degrade as occlusion increases; MegaPose ADD(-S) falls from 77.9 at low occlusion to 42.3 at high occlusion, and FFB6D to 13.2.

Unseen-object 2D detection degrades sharply under heavy occlusion, repeated instances and strong reflections (SAM6D drops more than 33% AP), detections get wrong object IDs in dense multi-instance scenes, and unseen-object pose depends on an upstream segmentation prior.
State-of-the-art pipelines need a separate pretrained detector or segmenter; end-to-end methods that integrate detection are needed.
Gen6D matches instance-specific estimators on LINEMOD only when given ground-truth bounding boxes.
Deep instance-level methods (CosyPose, SurfEmb, GDRNPP) score far below geometric PPF in clutter.

GraspClutter6D high occlusion / ADD(-S): FoundationPose 55.0, MegaPose 42.3 (77.9 at low occlusion), GDR-Net 27.7, FFB6D 13.2 (839)
