painpoints.attempted_fixes: Zero-shot proposal generators (CNOS, SAM-6D, NIDS-Net, MUSE); open-vocabulary segmenters (Grounded-SAM); ground-truth masks or boxes supplied to baselines (hides detection error); keypoint diffusion denoising (6D-Diff); geometric PPF matching; new clutter-heavy datasets; proposed adaptation of foundation segmentation to clutter, end-to-end detection plus pose, detection by local feature matching, occlusion-robust pose and better amodal detection.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Novel-object detectors and pose estimators are trained on lightly occluded, well-separated objects, in clutter the visible evidence per object becomes small and ambiguous, and benchmarks that supply ground-truth masks remove the pressure to solve detection.

painpoints.name: Multi-sensor synchronization, calibration and registration errors
painpoints.statement: Multi-sensor and casual capture rigs (multiple Kinects or RealSense, headset plus external cameras, camera plus LiDAR, mocap plus RGB domes, video plus IMU suits or insoles, phone plus depth camera) lack hardware synchronization and robust calibration, so they depend on claps, jumps, flashlights and manual alignment, and residual time offsets, rolling shutter, VIO initialisation and body-fit errors cap accuracy, especially for fast hand motion.
painpoints.description: Body-object dataset papers report Azure Kinect inter-camera delays that bound fitting error from below and produce hand jitter, HoloLens-Kinect misalignment visible on fast hand motion, sensors aligned to the slowest stream, clock drift and slipping head-mounted devices in long recordings, and camera-LiDAR frame drops that force offline work. Calibration is fragile: Kinect IR over-exposes on chessboards, chessboard calibration needs dense-matching refinement, broadcast cameras lack pre-game scans, and in-the-wild rigs trail wired systems in accuracy. Casual-capture papers add that several VIO systems cannot start without a static device, that rolling-shutter phones are calibrated with global-shutter models, that small phone-to-depth-camera offsets degrade poses, and that inaccurate SMPL fits misregister pixels and over-smooth reconstructions. Workarounds are sync events, manual start-frame labelling, software TCP sync, PTP hardware sync and 3D poses used as extra calibration constraints.

Hardware-level sync across RGB-D sensors is often missing, and small misalignments cause artifacts.

painpoints.why_it_persists: Commodity sensors have independent clocks, different frame rates and no shared trigger, and calibration targets suited to one modality fail on another. Sub-frame offsets are negligible for slow body motion but not for fast hand motion, so hand accuracy hits the rig's timing floor.

painpoints.name: Demonstration capture is costly, narrow and misses force-rich skills
painpoints.statement: Robot-side and wearable demonstration interfaces (kinesthetic teaching, teleoperation, handheld grippers, wearables) remain costly, slow and physically burdensome per demonstration and cannot record clean force-rich or fine flexible-object skills, so manipulation datasets stay narrow, mostly tabletop pick-and-place, static and unevenly covered.
painpoints.description: Kinesthetic teaching is too physically demanding for scale and its replay becomes jerky and misaligned under strong contact force; teleoperation without force feedback struggles with force-involved skills, is unsafe in contact-rich tasks and is costly and hardware-coupled; handheld grippers need at least 200 demonstrations per task at roughly twice bare-hand time with a 780 g tool. Grippers built for rigid pick-and-place cannot open thin flexible packaging, a force-torque sensor on a hand-held powered tool would impair ergonomics, and robot-mounted tools bias demonstrations through inertia. Wearable head and hand tracking needs fitting, calibration and synchronisation and is not mature for large-scale deployment. As a result robot and human manipulation datasets have restricted scene and task diversity, are small relative to vision-language corpora, are released as one-off static corpora with fragmented pipelines, and have uneven geographic and body-type coverage. Mixed modalities, redesigned fingers, haptic rendering, smartphone and head-mounted capture, generated data and community-extensible releases trade scale against fidelity and robot alignment.

painpoints.name: Non-robot data does not reliably improve robot policies
painpoints.statement: Human manipulation video and simulation-generated data do not reliably raise robot policy success: without task- and scene-aligned robot anchor data they give no gain or lower in-domain success, simulation data hurts simple in-domain tasks, and the exchange rate between teleoperation, simulation, human-video and other demonstration sources is task-dependent and cannot be predicted in advance.
painpoints.description: Human-video pretraining lowered in-domain success on all three bimanual tasks of one study (Pick Dual Bottles 0.70 to 0.45), neither diverse nor aligned human data alone gave significant gains in another, and latent actions and discrete tokens from human video helped only when robot data was scarce; 1,000 h of egocentric pretraining roughly matches 100 h of robot data. Simulation data hurts simple in-domain tasks through sim-to-real artifacts, generators cannot create new physics and repeat trajectories, simulators lack touch, and building simulated twins required scanning every object. Exchange rates between data sources are task- and goal-dependent, mixing ratios are set empirically, and heterogeneous action spaces and coordinate frames give conflicting supervision. Surveys explain the failures as under-grounding, mis-grounding and false visual equivalence. Task-aligned anchor data, budget-aware simulation mixing, robotized human video and large human-video-pretrained backbones help only with aligned or substantial robot data.

painpoints.name: Bimanual robot policies fail on coordination and handover
painpoints.statement: Learned bimanual and dexterous robot policies (imitation, RL, VLA) cannot reliably perform tightly coordinated two-arm tasks, arm-to-arm and human-to-robot handovers or sub-millimetre bimanual handling, even in noiseless simulation, and the policies that do well rely on perfect point clouds, simulator state or perfect perception of the partner's hand and object, so they collapse under realistic perception and sim-to-real transfer.
painpoints.description: Simulation benchmarks report average success well below 50 percent and near zero on handovers, stacking and coordinated lifts, and real dual-arm results stay low on precise, asymmetric or deformable tasks. Policies that do well in clean simulation rely on perfect point clouds, segmentation or state observations and collapse under domain randomization (RoboTwin 2.0 Easy to Hard: DP3 55.2 to 5.0 percent). Human-to-robot handover benchmarks assume perfect perception of hand and object states or non-reactive simulated givers, and dynamic handover success collapses in hard mode, where RGB-only policies cannot handle occlusion and depth ambiguity. Failures are attributed to arm collisions from poor spatial awareness or timing, missing coordination design and noisy multimodal demonstrations. Imitation learning at scale, LLM-generated simulation data, domain randomization, active perception, force sensing and human-video co-training give small gains.

painpoints.name: Wearable and non-visual sensing drifts and does not transfer
painpoints.statement: Body-worn IMUs, wrist sEMG, mmWave, Wi-Fi, thermal and IR arrays, event cameras and pressure mats cannot yet replace cameras for body and hand pose: inertial and EMG-derived estimates drift with time and distance, learned models lose much of their accuracy on unseen users, sensor units and rooms, accuracy stays below RGB or IMU suits, and the privacy these sensors are said to offer is not measured.
painpoints.description: Multi-modal datasets report Wi-Fi pose error rising from 147 to 399 mm across domains, mmWave error about twice the IMU error, IR-array and acoustic errors of 240-440 mm, and event-only input as the worst modality. Inertial capture drifts and needs recalibration, LiDAR or scene constraints, and IMU models lose most of their drift correction on a different IMU unit. sEMG relates to pose derivatives, so integrated pose drifts, and EMG models degrade across users and tasks while electrodes detach with perspiration. Pressure maps cannot localize limbs out of contact, and thermal residue confuses labels. A position paper argues that skeletons, depth and RF still leak identity and that no pose benchmark reports a privacy score, and fusion, personalization and domain adaptation are proposed but only partly shown.

sEMG models remain less accurate than vision methods; angular drift comes from velocity integration, and accuracy degrades most for held-out user plus held-out gesture combinations.
IMU-only estimation accumulates drift, and transfer to a different IMU cuts the integration-error reduction from about 90-92% to about 53-60%.
Non-RGB modalities still leak biometric identity through skeleton, shape and gait; obfuscation degrades joint precision; no standard privacy metric exists.
RGB is ineffective in darkness and under covers, LWIR heat residue causes labeling ambiguity, and the pressure map cannot localize limbs out of contact.

painpoints.name: Parametric body templates break on bodies that deviate from them
painpoints.statement: Pose, mesh and avatar pipelines built on SMPL or SMPL-X, linear blend skinning and a complete-limb, able-bodied template cannot represent loose clothing, residual limbs, prostheses, mobility aids or impaired movement, so fits twist, misalign or hallucinate limbs, an attached rigid device cannot be recovered with the body, and clinical models collapse across sites.
painpoints.description: Avatar papers report that body models built from subjects in tight-fit clothing fail when clothing covers most of the skin, that SMPL dependence limits loose clothing and may hurt the generalization of human NeRFs, and that earlier SMPL-X fits twisted and self-intersected. Inclusive-pose datasets show estimators putting keypoints on missing limbs, reading prostheses as natural ankles and propagating hallucinated limbs over time, while model-based estimators cannot represent an attached rigid prosthesis and model-free reconstruction lacks kinematic priors. Clinical gait and blind-pedestrian models degrade across sites and on cane and arm joints, severe cases are scarce, and synthetic datasets contain no amputees, children or assistive devices. New keypoint schemas, limb-deficiency-aware losses and small fine-tuning sets help locally, and SMPL-free encoders are proposed as future work.

painpoints.name: Human demonstrations cannot be aligned to the robot's observations
painpoints.statement: Human demonstrations cannot yet be brought into the robot's observation space: frame-aligned human-robot pairs cannot be captured at scale, rendering, inpainting, editing and video world models do not reliably replace the human actor or preserve contact, and demonstrations recorded from another viewpoint or place cannot be associated or transferred, so working methods assume identical cameras or mirrored workspaces.
painpoints.description: Fine human-robot alignment needs VR teleoperation in mirrored workspaces, handheld-gripper re-enactment of each demonstration or synthetic pseudo-references, and is restricted to pick-and-place. Generated robot videos show actor leakage, contact-region and contact-mode mismatch and omitted action events, general image editors fail embodiment and interaction preservation, render-and-inpaint pipelines ignore robot-scene occlusion and take tens of minutes per clip, and generic video-quality and VLM metrics do not detect these failures. Cross-view association is barely above random zero-shot, human video harms policies partly through viewpoint and spatial mismatch, and camera-robot alignment has a high-error tail under viewpoint inconsistency. Mirrored workspaces, UMI re-enactment, pseudo-pair pipelines with human screening, depth-corrected compositing, deployment-camera backgrounds and operator-selected virtual robot bases avoid the mismatch by construction rather than solving it.

painpoints.name: Symmetric objects make pose ambiguous and metrics inconsistent
painpoints.statement: Learned 6D pose estimators need object symmetries to be known and handled at training time, output a single deterministic pose where symmetry or partial observation makes the answer multimodal, and are scored by metrics (ADD, ADD-S, BOP symmetry definitions) that treat discrete and continuous symmetries inconsistently.
painpoints.description: Monocular pose surveys state that deep methods lose accuracy when visual symmetries are not considered during training and that symmetries usually must be supplied beforehand, yet symmetry transformations were not even available for MegaPose's training objects in BOP 2023. Generative pose models do not resolve the problem: energy-based aggregation in GenPose fails on the discontinuous multimodal distributions that discrete symmetries create, and non-symmetry-aware evaluation drops sharply on large vocabularies. Metric papers note that ADD over-estimates and ADD-S under-estimates error for symmetric objects, that the BOP symmetry definition depends on visual similarity, and that no metric covers finite and infinite ambiguity together. Pseudo-labelers also stay poor on symmetric bowls and industrial parts, and surveys call for uncertainty outputs instead of single deterministic poses.

evidence_items.item: Deep methods lose accuracy when visual symmetries are not considered at training time; symmetries often must be known beforehand, and uncertainty estimation for downstream decisions is open.
Energy-based aggregation (GenPose) fails on discontinuous multimodal distributions from discrete symmetries; ambiguity from symmetry and partial observation remains.
ADD over-estimates and ADD-S under-estimates error for symmetric objects; the BOP symmetry definition requires visual similarity.
A unified metric for objects with finite and infinite pose ambiguity is missing; ADD-S is not comparable to ADD, and IADD for infinite axes falls back to center distance.
Symmetry transformations are not available for MegaPose training objects.

benchmark_evidence: LINEMOD / ADD(S)-0.1d and Proj2D: OnePose++ on glue 48.0 and 51.8 (1325)
HOPE / BOP AR: evaluation needs MSSD/VSD/MSPD because ADD and ADD-S mis-estimate symmetric error (1315; no specific gap number)
painpoints.settings: Rigid household and industrial objects with discrete or continuous symmetry (bowls, cans, glue, metal parts) in RGB and RGB-D instance, category and unseen-object pose (LINEMOD, Omni6D, ROPE, HOPE, GraspNet-1Billion unseen benchmark, XYZ-IBD, IndustryShapes, BOP 2023) and DynOPETs pseudo-labels.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Symmetry-aware losses and metrics (ADD-S, BOP MSSD/MSPD) that need symmetry labels in advance, a sampled IADD metric, and generative diffusion or energy-based pose (GenPose, GenPose++), which still fails on discrete symmetries. Keypoint-based symmetry handling, new pose representations and uncertainty modelling are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Symmetry is a property of shape and texture that is unknown for novel objects, and single-output regression evaluated by single-pose metrics has no way to represent or reward the set of equivalent answers.

painpoints.name: Dynamic neural reconstruction fails under articulated motion and occlusion
painpoints.statement: Dynamic radiance-field, Gaussian and 4D generative reconstructions fail on manipulating hands, hand-held objects and moving people: interaction sequences score lower than object-only ones, ego-motion combined with near-range hand motion breaks dynamic novel-view synthesis, and quality drops with long sequences, fast hair or body motion, topology changes and even the involuntary sway of subjects asked to hold still.
painpoints.description: Dense-dome benchmarks report blurry, noisy hands and lower PSNR on hand-object sequences than on object-only ones, and egocentric multi-view data shows existing 3D and 4D NVS methods failing with ego-motion, near-range hand motion, large disparities and occlusion. For a static camera with a hand-rotated object, object poses are too inaccurate for NeRF or 3DGS to render the full object, and hand occlusion hides part of its appearance. Avatar papers report that deformation-field baselines struggle on long sequences with topology changes (HumanRF PSNR falling from 30.3 to 29.1 between 20 and 1000 frames), that dynamic NeRFs work only on short, limited-motion sequences, that video-diffusion 4D methods cannot represent large movements, and that per-frame masks flicker. Per-frame models lack temporal consistency, stereo guidance needs rectified stereo, pose refinement gives marginal gains, and motion priors and temporally consistent matting are left to future work.
source_clusters: G1_hoi_hands:Dynamic novel-view synthesis of hand-object scenes
G5_avatar_clinical:Long, fast or involuntary subject motion

evidence_items.item: All methods score lower on hand-object interaction sequences than object-only ones because of hand occlusion and complex hand motion; MixVoxels gives blurry, noisy hands.

Deformation-field baselines struggle on long sequences with complex motion and rapid topology changes; per-frame Instant-NGP lacks temporal stability; inconsistent per-frame masks cause silhouette-edge flicker; scaling dynamic representations to long sequences under memory budgets is open.

Existing 3D and 4D NVS methods fail with combined ego-motion, near-range hand motion, large disparities and frequent occlusions; dynamic models are designed for object-centric or fixed-pose multiview video.
Pose estimation from handheld sequences is inaccurate, so NeRF/3DGS cannot fully render the object, and hand occlusions hamper learning full appearance; pose refinement gives only marginal gains.
Dynamic NeRFs work on short sequences with limited motion; extremely fast hair motion yields blurry canonical hash-grid output; NHA preprocessing failed on 3 complex-motion sequences.
Subjects sway during the 11-second OLAT capture, blurring image-based relighting and requiring optical-flow motion compensation; the dataset covers static humans only.

benchmark_evidence: DiVa-360 / PSNR lower on interaction than object-only sequences by 2.73 dB (PF I-NGP), 1.98 dB (MixVoxels), 0.44 dB (K-Planes); 48-58 s training per frame (20)
ActorsHQ (4x downscaled, 8 actors), PSNR/LPIPS: HumanRF PSNR falls from 30.30 at 20 frames to 29.05 at 1000 frames; LPIPS rises from 0.095 to 0.107 [1437]
Ego-1K / held-out PSNR: K-Planes 16.46, per-frame 3DGS 21.22, Spacetime Gaussians 24.76, stereo-guided 3DGS 29.12 (226)
NVS-HO / median foreground PSNR about 16 for the best baseline (Splatfacto with COLMAP poses) (1103)
painpoints.settings: Table-scale 53-camera dome (DiVa-360), 12-camera egocentric head rig (Ego-1K), static camera with hand-rotated objects (NVS-HO), 51-view studio (GigaHands); full-body free-viewpoint video (ActorsHQ), dynamic heads (NeRSemble, RenderMe-360), OLAT light stage (HumanOLAT), handheld portraits (SmartPortraits), 4D human generation.
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Per-frame I-NGP (temporally inconsistent), stereo-guided 3DGS (needs rectified stereo), pose refinement during training (marginal), 4D feature decomposition with temporal partitioning, hash ensembles with deformation and optical-flow motion compensation. Pose-free feed-forward NVS, motion priors and consistent matting are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Dynamic neural fields assume either a canonical shape with smooth deformation or accurate per-frame camera and object poses; hand-object manipulation violates both through large articulation, contact-induced topology changes and occlusion, and memory budgets limit long sequences.

painpoints.name: Long-horizon and shifted conditions break learned policies
painpoints.statement: Policies trained from human, handheld or teleoperated demonstrations cannot complete long-horizon multi-stage manipulation and fail when object position, layout, pose, dynamics, camera or clutter change, because they rely on demonstration-aligned motion priors, lose the stage estimate under ambiguous views and accumulate small errors until tight tolerances fail.
painpoints.description: Real-world UMI benchmarks report zero full success on multi-stage and long-horizon rearrangement: policies lose the stage estimate when wrist observations look alike across stages or accumulate small placement deviations until a tight final tolerance fails, and chained-instruction benchmarks drop to near-zero success. Performance drops more under position, layout, pose and dynamics shifts than under object or appearance shifts and further under combined shifts, robot-only training fails in clutter, and baselines reach near-zero success on unseen objects or environments. Surveys cite compounding errors into states absent from demonstrations, spurious correlations from small datasets and a density-estimation objective that does not match task success, while human-video pipelines cover only short atomic skills. Splitting tasks, chain-of-thought conditioning (no benefit), large-scale pretraining, simulation co-training and tactile pretraining give partial gains.
source_clusters: G4_robot_learning:Long-horizon multi-stage tasks fail
G4_robot_learning:Policies degrade under geometric and dynamics shifts

evidence_items.item: All three evaluated policies get 0% full success on T3 (multi-stage) and T9 (long-horizon rearrangement); on T3 they lose the stage estimate under an ambiguous single wrist view, and on T9 small early placement deviations fail the tight final tolerance.
Robot-only training in cluttered multi-object scenes reaches 0.0 percent (200 clips) and 8.0 percent (500 clips) success.

With no fixed third-person view, similar wrist observations across stages confuse long-horizon inference; Diffusion Policy cannot handle long-horizon tasks, so tasks were split into subtasks, and errors accumulate over stages.
CALVIN success drops sharply for five sequential instructions, and multi-step logical tasks fail systematically on VLABench.
Compounding errors in sequential decisions push the robot into states absent from demonstrations; solving arbitrary long-horizon tasks remains open.
On LIBERO-plus camera and robot perturbations the tactile-pretrained model scores 48.9 and 49.5, below some baselines.

benchmark_evidence: UMI-Bench 1.0 T3 tool-mediated stamping (1372) / full success rate: 0 percent for all three models; best progress score 34.30.
UMI-Bench 1.0 all tasks (1372) / progress score: mean 59.62 seen/seen, 45.33 under Factor-B (position, layout, pose, dynamics) shifts, 40.19 under combined unseen object and position.
UMI-Bench 1.0 T9 long-horizon rearrangement (1372) / full success rate: 0 percent for all models; progress scores 10.6 to 26.4.
LIBERO-plus (1385) / zero-shot success under camera perturbation: 48.9 percent versus OpenVLA-OFT 56.4 and pi0-Fast 65.1.

FastUMI-100K Heat Food, Flexiv Rizon4 with pi0 (1369) / stage success: put bread into microwave 0.00 percent and close door 0.00 percent after 100 percent door opening; Wash Clothes close washer door 60.00 percent.
painpoints.settings: Real tabletop and household tasks with UMI-style wrist-fisheye observations and VLA or diffusion policies (UMI-Bench, FastUMI-100K); simulated chained-instruction and robustness suites (CALVIN, VLABench, LIBERO-plus, THE COLOSSEUM); egocentric procedural planning (EgoExoLearn); real robots under unseen object, position, layout, background, camera and clutter conditions (WIYH, HuRo ALLEX, Aloha-Agilex, Unitree G1, UR5 with dexterous hands, CosmoH2G).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Splitting tasks into subtasks; chain-of-thought conditioning (no benefit); large-scale human-video or robotized pretraining; simulation co-training; tactile pretraining; proposed LLM planning grounded in skills, fusion of UMI-style and conventional data, closed-loop feedback with collision-aware planning, structured priors and 3D feature fields.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Imitation policies learn the state distribution of their demonstrations and have no mechanism to recover from compounding deviations, and the demonstration data is short, narrow and lacks explicit task-stage and 3D state structure.

painpoints.name: Photoreal avatars of new people without studio capture
painpoints.statement: Photorealistic, driveable head, hand and body avatars cannot yet be built for a new person from phone, headset or monocular input, nor driven to expressions and poses outside those captured, because studio fidelity still needs per-subject capture in calibrated domes, models are fitted per identity, and high-fidelity human capture data is scarce and too large to distribute.
painpoints.description: Avatar reference models are built on domes of 16 to about 230 synchronized cameras, reconstruction error rises as training cameras are removed, and paired dome, headset and phone captures exist for only four subjects, so headset driving relies on pseudo ground truth from personalized avatars. Head and body avatar models are optimized per identity or sequence (about one day on eight V100 GPUs per face identity), generalizable models learn mean priors that fail on unseen identities, rare poses and complex garments, novel-expression methods fail on out-of-distribution expressions, and free-viewpoint models have no articulation control outside training poses. High-fidelity human capture data is far smaller than object-centric 3D data, petabyte-scale captures cannot be distributed at full fidelity, and their creators train on only part of them. Larger multi-view datasets, tiered and compressed releases, cycle-consistency headset drivers and priors learned from high-end captures are tried or proposed.
source_clusters: G5_avatar_clinical:Avatars from lightweight sensors need studio capture
G5_avatar_clinical:Per-identity fitting without cross-identity generalization
G5_avatar_clinical:Driving avatars beyond captured expressions and poses
G5_avatar_clinical:Scarce, small and undistributable human capture data

evidence_items.item: The field cannot yet build relightable, multi-identity, full-body driveable avatars from commodity sensors without per-subject high-end dome captures; only the 4 Goliath subjects carry the full paired capture, which restricts research on converting low-quality captures to high quality.
Unseen-identity NVS causes a larger performance drop than unseen-expression NVS; generalizable methods learn mean-head priors but fail on long-tail cases.
Future work: dynamic NeRFs that generalize over identities and expressions instead of per-sequence fitting.
Experiments use 62% of the data due to size, hardware and annotation constraints.
Reconstruction error rises as training cameras drop from 37 to 17 views; data-hungry neural face models need dense high-resolution multi-view captures (40 to 160 cameras).
HumanRF requires the high-end ActorsHQ capture (160 synchronized 12 MP cameras); future work is training on high-end recordings to build avatars driven from monocular-only test sequences.

benchmark_evidence: Multiface (identity m-20180227), screen-space reconstruction error: joint novel view plus novel expression 1.088 with 37 training cameras rising to 1.272 with 17, versus 0.770 for novel view only at 37 cameras [1431]

RenderMe-360 Generalizable NVS (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): the unseen-ID protocol shows a larger drop than the unseen-expression protocol for IBRNet, VisionNeRF and KeypointNeRF (the digest gives no single number) [1432]
RenderMe-360 Novel Expression (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/L1): NeRFace, IM Avatar and PointAvatar all fail on OOD expressions such as tongue out [1432]
Goliath-4, number of subjects: only 4 subjects carry the full 8-modality paired capture [1430, 438]
Ava-256 release: 2x or 4x downsampled resolution, about 80 of about 170 cameras, 7.5 or 15 fps instead of 30 fps, to fit 4 to 32 TB releases [1430, 438]
painpoints.settings: Multi-view studio domes (Multiface 40-160 cameras, Codec Avatar Studio about 170 and about 230 cameras, ActorsHQ 160 cameras, NeRSemble 16 cameras, RenderMe-360 60 cameras, MVHumanNet and MVHumanNet++) contrasted with lightweight inputs (Quest Pro headset IR cameras, phone scans, handheld smartphone plus Azure Kinect); generalizable human NeRF and feed-forward reconstruction; text-driven avatar generation; scan-based avatar training (MVP-Human); light-stage capture (HumanOLAT).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Paired dome, headset and phone releases (Ava-256, Goliath) and cycle-consistency headset drivers for personalized avatars; larger multi-view datasets for generalizable NeRFs and feed-forward models; tiered, downsampled and compressed releases; partial-data training and synthetic substitutes (artifacts); expression-conditioned implicit and point avatars; proposed priors learned from high-end captures for monocular driving, generalizable encoders and parametric articulation control.
painpoints.why_it_persists: Photoreal, driveable avatars need dense, identity-specific appearance and expression data that only studio domes provide, and that data is too costly to capture and too large to share at the scale cross-identity generalization requires.

painpoints.name: Hair, thin structures and light transport are not modelled
painpoints.statement: Even with dense studio input, human avatar methods cannot reconstruct or render fast or curly hair, thin structures, teeth and the occluded mouth interior, eye specularities and refraction, nor relight people with subsurface scattering, self-shadowing and sharp shadows, and relightable training data exist for only a few subjects in static poses.
painpoints.description: Head-capture datasets report poorly reconstructed teeth and eyelashes, sharp drops on curly hair and complex accessories, blur building up in dynamic hair, hollow-mouth artifacts, and unmodelled eye specularity and refraction. Relighting benchmarks find that the best Gaussian inverse-rendering methods stay blurry and miss specular highlights and sharp shadows, and that harmonization methods lack subsurface scattering and self-shadows. Relightable data exist only for 21 static subjects in a light stage and four dome subjects, and many datasets capture under uniform diffuse light and exclude relighting. Deformation fields with hash ensembles, adapted inverse-rendering methods and new OLAT datasets fall short.
source_clusters: G5_avatar_clinical:Hair, mouth interior, eyes and accessories in head avatars
G5_avatar_clinical:Full-body relighting and relightable data scarcity

evidence_items.item: Teeth and eyelashes are poorly reconstructed; the baseline fails on high-frequency details; prior mesh-based Codec Avatars fall short on thin structures, translucency and biological motion.

Evaluated Gaussian inverse-rendering methods stay blurry and miss specular highlights and sharp shadows; IC-Light harmonization rarely produces self-shadows and fails to preserve eye color and mouth shape; PRT-Gaussian fails to reconstruct geometry from OLAT frames, producing ghosting.

Hair rendering degrades sharply for curly hair; all static NVS methods drop as accessory complexity increases; IM Avatar struggles with thin structures like hair bands and strands; NR-NeRF blur accumulates across frames in dynamic hair.
The deformation field cannot capture fast hair motion; teeth are reconstructed at the back of the mouth under heavy occlusion; eye specular reflections cause artifacts; refraction is not modelled.

The release is unlikely to support multi-identity relightable head decoders since relightable data exist only for the four Goliath subjects; relightable capture needs time-multiplexed group-light illumination.

benchmark_evidence: RenderMe-360 Hair Rendering (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): the curls subset causes sharp drops under all metrics for static and dynamic NVS methods [1432]

HumanOLAT novel view plus novel light (PSNR/LPIPS/SSIM, Table 2, six captures): methods that do well on object-centric scenes give blurry renderings with hand and face artifacts (the digest gives no single number) [1439]
RenderMe-360 Single-ID NVS (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS): Instant-NGP, NeuS, NV and MVP all drop with deformable and complex accessories [1432]
HumanOLAT illumination harmonization (qualitative): IC-Light lacks subsurface scattering and self-shadowing and loses facial details [1439]
NeRSemble (10 sequences, 4 held-out views, extreme viewing angles), PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS: 31.8 / 0.875 / 0.212 versus DyNeRF 30.6 / 0.860 / 0.254, with residual hair and mouth artifacts [1436]
painpoints.settings: Dense multi-view head capture (Multiface, RenderMe-360, NeRSemble), light-stage OLAT capture (HumanOLAT, 21 subjects, 3 static poses), relightable head dome (Goliath, 4 subjects), uniform-light face dome (Multiface).
painpoints.attempted_fixes: Deformation fields with hash ensembles, NeRF, point and implicit avatars, adapted PRT-Gaussian, IntrinsicAvatar and IC-Light, optical-flow motion compensation and new OLAT datasets. Hair motion priors and learned 4D priors for occluded regions are proposed.
painpoints.why_it_persists: These effects need physically based light transport and fine geometry that current neural representations approximate poorly, and measuring them requires light stages with time-multiplexed illumination that few labs have.

notes:
I reconciled merger A (mechanism lens, 39 pain points) with merger B (capability lens, 38) into 40 pain points: 22 core, 15 adjacent and 3 peripheral, ordered by n_papers within each relevance tier. A script (scratchpad w3r/build.py, output w3r/final.json) checked the result. Each of the 110 group clusters appears in exactly one source_clusters list. The union of paper_ids across the 40 points equals the union across all clusters: 293 records, with the uncategorized 1542, 1544 and 1545 left out. Every evidence item is verbatim from a source cluster of its own pain point, comes from a distinct paper and never uses both ids of a duplicate pair. Every source cluster contributes at least one evidence item, and all text is ASCII.

Paper ids. Re-reading the maps showed that both mergers' paper_ids already equalled the union of their source clusters. Every id disagreement was therefore a disagreement about which pain point a cluster belongs to. Final paper_ids were recomputed from the maps for each final cluster set. n_papers counts distinct works, so the five known duplicate record pairs count once: 67/1456 (OakInk2), 1035/1191 (Bi-DexHands), 348/1316 (PACE), 438/1430 (Codec Avatar Studio) and 434/1562 (Muscles in Time). This follows A's convention; B counted records. paper_ids keep both ids of each pair.

Agreement. Both lists built 14 pain points from the same cluster set. For each I kept the sharper statement and unioned the evidence. I used A's text for fast motion (P22), contact (P13), articulated objects (P14), commodity depth (P10), ground truth (P01), pseudo-labels (P19), force (P26), wearable sensing (P33), dynamic reconstruction (P37), actions (P27) and embodiment (P23). I used B's text for template-free objects (P02), domain gap (P21) and metrics (P06).

Splits kept. Each part rests on at least 4 papers and names a distinct cause or capability.
(1) A's 'mutual occlusion' (76 papers) is split as in B into finger pose under occlusion (P15) and handled-object pose (P04). The cause is shared but the capability differs.
(2) B's 'two hands and several agents' (71 papers) is split as in A into two hands and close bodies confused (P09) and single-hand, single-agent scope (P17). The first is caused by self-similar overlap and identity; the second by restricted data and method scope.
(3) B's object-property point is split as in A. Symmetry (P36, 12 papers; cause: shape ambiguity and metric definition) stands apart from texture, material and size (P12).
(4) A's 'brittle policies' is split as in B into bimanual coordination and handover (P32) and long-horizon and shift failures (P38). P32 carries the assumption of perfect perception of the hand and object, which ties it to tracking.
Real-time (P03) and temporal continuity (P20) were separate in both lists and stay separate.

Splits not kept. Keeping both of the following would have given 42 points, over the 40 cap, and these were the weakest distinctions.
(5) A's standalone unseen-object detection is merged with G3 clutter occlusion, as in B (P28). Both come from low visible evidence per object in clutter, and the detection evidence itself is about occlusion and repeated instances.
(6) A's 'datasets small, narrow and hard to distribute' is dissolved into B's structure. G4 narrow manipulation datasets joined demonstration capture (P30), since narrowness is attributed to acquisition cost (for example, 1388). G5 scarce human capture data joined studio-capture avatars (P39). A's version joined robot corpora and avatar captures only through data scarcity.

Single-cluster disagreements, settled by re-reading the cluster statements:
- G1 'No causal, temporally stable tracking' went to real-time, P03 (as in B). Its statement ends with offline smoothing that cannot run causally.
- G5 clinical finger kinematics went to finger pose, P15 (as in B). It names occlusion and few viewpoints.
- G5 'Monocular depth ambiguity and self-occlusion' went to body occlusion, P11 (as in B). Four of its six items concern unobservable self-occluded regions.
- G2 body occlusion and G2 close-range views went to P11 (as in B), not with G3 clutter (as in A).
- G4 world models went to physical consistency, P18 (as in A). Its named defect is physical invalidity.
- G4 simulation data went to non-robot data value, P31 (as in B). The defect is measured as policy success, and A's own data-value point already names simulated data.
- G5 camera and body-pose registration went to sync and calibration, P29 (as in A). Its items are time offsets, rolling-shutter calibration and SMPL-fit misregistration.
- G4 paired human-robot demonstrations went to observation alignment, P35 (as in B). Pixel-aligned pairs are the missing correspondence for visual conversion.
- G5 clinical validity went to benchmarks, P25 (as in A). It is a validation problem and has only 3 papers.
- G5 tight-fit body priors joined G2 atypical bodies in parametric templates, P34 (as in A). They share the template-topology cause. Hair and light transport stay separate (P40, 5 papers).

Text edits. I rewrote P32's statement to remove long-horizon content that now sits in P38, and I renamed P11 and P20. All other text comes from the merger whose pain point had the same cluster set: A for P01, P07, P09, P10, P12, P13, P14, P17, P18, P19, P22, P23, P24, P25, P26, P27, P29, P33, P34, P36, P37 and P40; B for the rest.

Relevance tags. P11 (body occlusion) is core, as in B; A had tagged it adjacent because its version included static clutter. P38 (long-horizon) is peripheral, as in B. P36 (symmetry) and P28 (clutter) are adjacent. Force (P26), sync (P29) and wearable sensing (P33) are adjacent in both lists.

Evidence. Each pain point has 5 or 6 evidence items, capped at 6 to limit payload size; the full lists remain in the maps. Items were chosen round-robin over source clusters, with the mergers' own choices first. Each point has up to 5 benchmark strings, chosen round-robin over source clusters and copied verbatim. G5 benchmark strings carry the source id in brackets, following A's convention; I added ids 1427, 1424 and 1436 after checking them in the G5 digest. Benchmark numbers were not recomputed.

Caveats carried over. The step-3a G3 notes say that P02, P14 and P28 include papers that only assume the condition, so their counts are inflated. P01 (ground truth) is broad because nearly every dataset paper states this cost.
